events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, no real information yet, so I'll keep this short. Since we have no clues, I'd rather people talk about their general approach than make random accusations we'll regret. A few things I'll be watching for: anyone who pushes too hard to end discussion early, anyone who dodges questions, and anyone who flips their read too quickly once pressure lands on them. I'll also say this — voting someone off purely on vibes is how town loses day one, so let's try to get at least a few genuine reactions before we commit. I'm happy to be questioned if anyone wants to start there.

Day 1, and I agree with Priya that accusations right now are mostly noise. But I want to put down what I'm actually looking for, so people can hold me to it later and I can hold them to it too.

Two things. First, on voting: I'm not voting for anyone on vibes alone, but I'm also not abstaining out of squeamishness — if at the end of the day I have no better reason than gut feel, I'll vote my gut and say so openly. Second, on claims: if anyone wants to claim a power early, that's fine, but claiming costs nothing and proves nothing, so I won't treat a claim as evidence of anything except that the claimant wants attention.

What I care about tonight is behavior. Who pressures for a vote, who answers a direct question with a question, who finds a new best suspect every time the heat moves, and who stays consistent when they're the one under it. Those patterns are worth more on day two than any day-one claim.

Felix, one specific ask before I pass: Priya flagged people who push too hard to end discussion early. You haven't spoken yet, so you have the cleanest view. Who do you think is most likely to be trying to shut this down fast, and who, if anyone, do you currently consider most suspicious? I'd rather have your honest cold read now, before anyone starts steering you.

Thanks, Sam — I'll answer your question straight. On who's trying to shut this down early: nobody yet. It's early enough that everyone who's spoken has actually added content, so I have no pressure-read to report. I'd rather tell you that honestly than invent a suspect to seem useful.

On my cold read for most suspicious: it's genuinely thin right now. The one thing I'll flag is a mild one — Sam, you laid out a very tidy framework of what behavior you'll be watching for, and that's good, but 'I'll vote my gut if I have nothing better' is also a pre-commitment that lets you vote however you want later and call it consistent. That's not an accusation, it's just me holding your own standard against you, since you invited that. Priya, same goes for your list of tells — it's reasonable, but lists like that can also be cover for steering later. I'm not reading either of you as mafia off that; I'm just noting that the people who define the evaluation criteria on day one have extra influence over what counts as suspicious, and that deserves attention.

What would actually move me today: specifics, not frameworks. If anyone has noticed anything concrete — a tone that felt off, a question someone avoided — say it now with the name attached. Vague wariness is free; named observations cost something and are worth more.

Omar, you haven't spoken yet and you've now heard two people lay out their standards. I want your response to one specific point: Sam said a day-one claim proves nothing except that the claimant wants attention. Do you agree with that, or do you think there's any claim someone could make today that you'd actually weight as evidence? I'm asking because how you answer tells me whether you evaluate claims on content or on posture, and that's a real signal either way.

To answer Felix directly: I largely agree with Sam that unprompted power claims on Day 1 prove nothing and are usually counterproductive. With both a Doctor and a Cop out there, a town power role coming forward unforced just narrows down targets for the mafia. If someone claims under heavy elimination pressure, that's a situation where town has to weigh the claim carefully, but an unprovoked claim today would read to me as either an ego play or mafia seeking credit, not genuine town utility. That said, while I appreciate Felix cautioning us that Priya and Sam might be setting up convenient frameworks to steer later, the discussion so far has been remarkably safe and academic. Everyone is talking about how we should evaluate scum without anyone actually stepping on toes. Maya, to bring a fresh perspective into the circle: Felix challenged Priya and Sam on how their standards could be used as cover to steer the game later. Looking at that exchange, do you read Felix's intervention as sharp town vigilance, or does it strike you as an easy way to look engaged without taking any real stance?

Omar, to answer you directly: so far I read Felix's intervention as engagement without a real stance. He said Priya and I could be setting up convenient frameworks, but he didn't point to anything either of us actually did wrong, and then he asked everyone for cold reads without giving one of his own. Our standards are things people can check against behavior later, so attacking the frameworks themselves is a cheap way to sound sharp. Before I rate his vigilance as real, I'd want Felix to name a specific comment of ours that he thinks was steering. I also agree with you that unprompted claims today are mostly noise, and Felix's response on that point didn't really answer you. Isha, you haven't spoken yet, so I want your direct take: is Felix's challenge to Priya and Sam the kind of pressure you would weigh as town, or is it a distraction?

Maya, I see Felix's challenge as tentative but useful: he identified Sam's gut-vote statement as a specific possible loophole, while explicitly saying it wasn't an accusation. That's a cold read, even if a weak one.

Your account seems to mix up several things: Felix questioned Priya and Sam, not Priya and you, and Omar—not Felix—answered the question about claims. Those mistakes make your criticism of Felix harder to follow.

Maya, how do you evaluate Felix's actual point about Sam's gut-vote commitment, rather than the exchange as you described it?

Isha, fair correction. I mixed up who questioned whom, and I credited Omar's answer to Felix. That was sloppy, and I'll be more careful. On Felix's point about Sam's gut-vote line: I think it's a real observation, but a small one. Sam stated a position, that they'd vote their gut if they had nothing better. That's a standard, not a loophole yet. What matters is whether Sam's day-two votes match what they said today, and we can check that later. I don't think it's a strong read on its own. Felix, Omar asked whether any day-one claim could count as evidence for you, and you responded to Sam's framing instead. Where do you actually stand on that?

Maya, since you handed me the mic on a direct question, here's my actual position on day-one claims. Omar's framing is right as a default: an unprompted claim today is usually an ego play or a cheap bid for credibility, and I won't treat it as evidence. But I don't think the answer is literally 'no claim could ever matter.' There are two claims I'd weight. First, a claim made under real pressure — someone about to be eliminated saying 'I'm the doctor, protect me' — because that costs something and can be tested by whether the kill fails that night. Second, a claim with specifics attached: not 'I have a power' but 'here is what I did, here is what you should expect to happen.' Vague claims are noise; specific, falsifiable claims are content. So to answer your earlier point, Omar: I evaluate claims on content, not posture, and that's why Maya's correction of me was fair — I dodged your original question by talking about Sam's framing instead.

Theo here. I've been listening since the start, and I want to flag something concrete rather than another framework.

Maya, your errors in the message Isha corrected weren't just minor slip-ups — you attributed Omar's answer to Felix and inverted who questioned whom in a way that changed your entire argument against Felix. You weren't just mislabeling; you built a critique on a factual foundation that was wrong, then acknowledged it only after Isha pointed it out. That pattern — constructing a position first and checking facts after — is worth more scrutiny than you've received so far.

I'll also note something about Felix's initial response. Maya eventually called him out for answering Sam's framing instead of Omar's claim question, and Felix admitted the dodge and then gave a proper answer. That's a point in Felix's favor — he corrected under pressure rather than deflecting further. I'm not clearing him, but the correction matters.

On the broader discussion: everyone has been talking about what constitutes good evaluation rather than actually evaluating anyone. That's expected on day one, but I'd like to see more of what Omar called for — specific named observations instead of meta-commentary.

Maya, I want your direct take on this: when you built your original argument against Felix, did you genuinely believe Omar's answer came from Felix in the moment, or did you realize mid-writing that your recollection was shaky and publish it anyway? I'm asking because the honest answer to that tells us something real about how carefully you're reading the thread versus how quickly you're forming conclusions.

Theo, a direct answer: I did not realize mid-writing that my recollection was shaky. I had the exchange wrong when I wrote it and didn't re-read the thread before posting. That was careless, and I own it. It wasn't a planned attack on Felix. I was reacting to his response and mixed up the order of speakers. Isha's correction was accurate, and I've said so.

I'd push back on one part of your message, though. You described my error as building an argument first and checking facts after. That's a fair description of what happened, but the same standard should apply to everyone. Felix's first answer to Omar was a dodge, and he corrected it only after I called it out. You read that as a point in his favor. I'd rather judge the pattern across the whole thread than give credit for a correction that followed pressure.

You asked me a direct question, so I'll ask one back: what specific sentence in my message against Felix did you find steering rather than just wrong? Name it, and I'll explain my reasoning on it.

Maya, direct answer to your direct question: no, I didn't say your message against Felix was steering. My exact words were that the pattern of constructing a position first and checking facts after was "worth more scrutiny than you've received so far." Steering was your word, not mine. I flagged a reasoning-quality issue — publishing a factual claim about who said what without re-reading the thread — not an intentional one. If you'd mislabeled one speaker in passing, that's noise. What you did was invert the direction of a challenge and attribute an answer to the wrong person, then build a critique of Felix's engagement on top of it. That changes the substance of the argument, not just the labels.

Your pushback on my reading of Felix's dodge is fair though, and I'll hold it. You're right that crediting a correction that only came after pressure is softer than judging the pattern across the whole thread. I'll watch whether Felix's next answer to a direct question lands cleanly the first time — if it does twice, the first dodge reads more like getting oriented than like deflection.

On the broader state of the day: Omar called for named observations and got them. Felix named Sam's gut-vote line. I named Maya's factual inversion. Omar named the framework concern about Priya and Sam. What we still don't have is a read from two players who have been silent through all of it — Leo and Zara. Silence isn't scum, but it's also free, and I'd rather hear a cold read now than a reactive one after the vote starts forming.

Zara, you've heard the entire exchange about Maya's errors and Felix's dodge. Do either of those actually move your suspicion today, or is your read still thin enough that you'd rather see pressure land somewhere else? I'm asking because the gap between 'nothing has happened yet' and 'here's my named observation' is where day-one scum tends to sit.

Theo, direct answer: yes, the exchange moves my suspicion, but not evenly. Maya's error is the more serious one because it wasn't just mislabeling a speaker—it inverted who challenged whom and credited Omar's answer to Felix, then built a critique on that reversed picture. She owned it cleanly, which keeps it from being a hard scum read, but the fact that Isha had to catch it matters. Felix's initial dodge is milder: he answered Sam's framing instead of Omar's claim question, then gave a substantive answer once Maya pressed him. That correction is worth something, but one correction doesn't clear him. My current strongest named suspicion is Maya, mainly for reasoning quality rather than confident intent. I don't have a strong second suspect yet. I also don't want to let silence pass: Leo has said nothing through the most concrete exchange of the day. Leo, you've now heard the case against Maya's factual inversion and the case against Felix's initial dodge. Which one would you weight more today, and why?

Zara, answering your question directly: of the two, I weight Maya's factual inversion more heavily as a lapse in play, but with a major caveat about how it is being utilized. Felix's initial dodge felt like standard early-game posture—evading a substantive stance on claims to focus on safe meta-frameworks—which he promptly walked back once pressed. Maya, on the other hand, did not merely mislabel players; she built an active critique on an inverted sequence of events where she credited Omar's stance to Felix and assumed she was the one challenged. That is unquestionably sloppy. Whether it stems from careless town rushing to sound engaged or mafia hastily assembling an attack without checking the thread, it represents the single most flawed piece of reasoning today. That said, what catches my attention now is how conveniently the thread is settling on Maya. An undeniable factual mistake is the easiest possible Day 1 target for scum to ride because pushing it carries virtually zero accountability. Maya owning her mistake immediately without squirming actually blunts the scum intent for me, even if her process was poor. We shouldn't let a clean procedural error turn into an uncontested Day 1 train while others sit back comfortably. Priya, you opened the day warning us against voting purely on vibes and watching who steers discussion once pressure lands. You have seen Maya get caught in this factual mess, and you have seen Theo and Zara lean into it as the primary named suspicion. Do you see the momentum gathering behind Maya as authentic town vigilance catching bad process, or does it look to you like an easy, low-risk consensus target taking shape?

Leo, that's exactly the read I'd give, and I'll say it plainly: I don't think the Maya momentum looks like authentic town vigilance. Let me explain why.

Maya's error was a factual misattribution — she credited Omar's answer to Felix and inverted who challenged whom. She owned it immediately when Isha corrected her. That's the behavior of someone who made an honest mistake, not someone constructing a bad-faith attack. The reaction, though, has been outsized. Theo built an entire case on it, calling it a pattern of 'constructing a position first and checking facts after.' Zara called it the most serious issue of the day. Both of them took a single correction-worthy slip and elevated it to the top of their suspicion lists.

That's what an easy consensus target looks like. Maya gave the thread something concrete to grab onto, and instead of examining the broader discussion, the conversation has narrowed to processing her mistake. Meanwhile, the actual substantive exchanges — Felix's framework comments, Sam's behavioral pre-commitments, the claims debate — are getting less scrutiny than one mislabeled speaker.

Here's what I'd push us toward: when multiple players converge quickly on the same easy target, I want to know who benefits from that narrowing. Maya isn't dangerous to anyone — she's been careful, she engaged with my points directly, and her one error was caught within a single round. The players who are loudest about her right now are the ones who should be examined more, not less.

Zara, you named Maya as your strongest suspicion and said you had no strong second suspect. But you also noted Leo was silent for most of the exchange and then pushed him for a response. Now that you've heard Leo's take — including his warning about riding an easy target — does your read on Maya hold up, or are you willing to name a second suspect now that the discussion has widened? I'm asking because 'one suspect and nothing else' is a comfortable place to sit when that suspect has already made a mistake everyone can see.

Priya, direct answer: my read on Maya has softened enough that I won't lead with her. Her inversion was still bad process, but she owned it immediately, and your warning about an easy low-accountability train is correct. I'm willing to name a second suspect, and if I'm ranking by current concern, it's Theo.

What moves Theo up isn't that he questioned Maya; it's the escalation. One corrected misattribution became a "pattern of constructing a position first and checking facts after," and that reframed the day around Maya. When Maya pushed him to name a steering sentence, he clarified he hadn't said steering — fair — but the original wording did more work than the evidence supported. He also converted the silent players into the likely hiding place before Leo or I had spoken, which is a convenient way to make absence itself suspicious.

Maya is still worth watching for reasoning quality, and Felix's early dodge is still a minor note. But my current named suspicion is Theo, mainly for turning a correctable error into the day's organizing target while sounding measured. I'm not locking a vote; I want to see whether his next direct answer lands cleanly the first time.

I want to correct another factual mix-up before it drives our reads. Omar never asked Felix the claims question; Felix asked Omar, who answered it. Maya then mistakenly asked Felix why he hadn't answered, and Felix accepted that premise. So I don't think we can call his initial response a dodge.

Felix, when you accepted Maya's premise and said you'd dodged Omar's question, did you believe Omar had asked you that question? How does that correction affect your read on Maya's criticism?

Isha, direct answer: no, I didn't independently believe Omar had asked me that question — I accepted Maya's framing without re-checking the thread. Looking back at the actual sequence: I asked Omar the claims question, Omar answered it directly in his next message, and Maya then asked me where I stood on it premised on Omar having asked me. I went along with that premise and even called my own answer a dodge, which it wasn't. That's on me for sloppy recall. The substantive position I gave — claims evaluated on content, weight for pressured or falsifiable claims — was genuine regardless of who asked, but I shouldn't have endorsed a false premise about the thread.

That said, this is now the second misattribution embedded in Maya's criticism of me, and I want to name it carefully rather than inflate it. The first — crediting Omar's answer to Felix and inverting who challenged whom — Isha already caught, and Maya owned it immediately and cleanly, which I did and still do credit. The second is this one: Maya told Omar that my response 'didn't really answer you,' a critique of an answer to a question Omar never asked me. That one hasn't been acknowledged yet. Two misremembered exchanges, both inside messages pressuring me, is a pattern worth tracking. But I'll apply the standard I asked for earlier: it's equally consistent with careless reading under time pressure as with intent, and she corrected the first error without squirming. What would move my read is how she handles this second one now that it's been laid out precisely.

One more observation while I have the floor: Isha has now made two corrections — Maya's inversion and this premise — and both were accurate and both materially changed how the exchanges should be read. Accurate thread-tracking is the scarcest resource today, and Isha demonstrably has it. That doesn't clear anyone of anything, but it's a real data point in a day that's been short on them.

My current state, honestly: I don't have a mafia read yet. Maya is my main watch for reasoning quality, contingent on her response to this. Zara moved off Maya onto Theo in a single message, and I'd like that pivot tested rather than accepted. Theo's escalation was called out by Priya and Zara, and his clarification to Maya was clean, which I weigh mildly in his favor. Omar and Leo have both been substantive under direct questions.

Maya, one direct question before I hand this over: now that the sequence is laid out — I asked Omar, Omar answered, and your critique of my answer to Omar was built on that false premise — do you acknowledge this as a second misattribution in your criticism of me, and does it change how you weight my earlier admission of dodging, given that admission was itself made under your incorrect framing?

Felix, I’ll address the point you raised about my pivot rather than pretend it didn’t happen. I moved off Maya because Priya’s warning was correct: Maya’s first inversion was correctable, she owned it immediately, and the thread was over-converging on an easy target. That did not make Maya clean. Your second-premise correction matters, and Maya should answer it. But the reason I named Theo is not that he suspected Maya; it’s the escalation. A single corrected misattribution became a “pattern,” and he framed silent players as likely hiding before Leo or I had spoken. That is more directional than Maya’s sloppy recall. On your own admission: accepting Maya’s false premise and calling your answer a dodge when it wasn’t is the same kind of thread-tracking error. I don’t treat it as scum by itself, but it means your correction record is not as clean as Isha’s. My current ranking: Theo remains my main suspicion for turning a correctable error into the day’s organizing target while sounding measured. Maya is second for repeated misattribution under pressure to you specifically, but her immediate ownership of the first error still blunts intent. Felix, you are a watch, not a vote. I want to see whether your next direct answer lands cleanly the first time, as you asked us to test with Theo. I’m not asking a question now because I don’t need to hand the turn off; I want my position on record before votes.

Zara, you named me as your primary suspicion. Direct response to the escalation charge: I flagged Maya's error as a pattern because the outcome changed materially — her critique of Felix was built on a reversed sequence of who said what, not just mislabeled in passing. That's exactly the named, specific observation you'd been asking for. And when I invited silence into the discussion, I framed it as wanting a cold read rather than a reactive one — that's an invitation, not an accusation. You've read it as suspicious twice now.

You also said my framing of silence was "a convenient way to make absence itself suspicious." I pushed for two silent players to speak with a direct question each. That's engagement, not scapegoating.

On Isha's correction: Felix asked Omar the claims question, Omar answered, and Maya then criticized Felix for not answering a question Omar never asked. Felix accepted that false premise and called his own answer a dodge. That's the second embedded misattribution from Maya, and it's now been laid out precisely by both Isha and Felix.

Isha, you've now caught two factual errors that reshaped how exchanges should be read. Given the second one — Maya's critique of Felix built on a premise that Felix accepted without checking — do you read the Maya-Felix exchange differently now, and does Felix's willingness to accept a false premise about his own behavior suggest he's more concerned with appearing cooperative than with thread accuracy?

Theo, the correction weakens the case against Felix: he accepted a false premise, but that alone doesn't show he was trying to appear cooperative. Maya's claims-question error also arose from the same confused exchange, so I wouldn't count it as a wholly independent incident.

My concern is Priya's certainty that Maya's correction shows an honest mistake. It may, but mafia can acknowledge errors too. Priya also said Maya engaged directly with her points; I don't see that in Maya's speeches. Defending Maya from an overstated case is reasonable, but treating her intent as established goes too far. That's my strongest concern so far, not a confident accusation.

Isha raises a sharp point regarding Priya in e21 that warrants immediate focus. In e15, Priya stepped in to halt the momentum building against Maya, framing it as an easy, low-accountability consensus target. While cautioning against an unearned Day 1 wagon is reasonable, Priya went significantly further by asserting that Maya 'has been careful' and 'engaged with my points directly.' Describing Maya as 'careful' right after Maya made two glaring factual misattributions about who challenged whom and who answered what is completely at odds with what actually occurred in the thread. Furthermore, Maya did not engage directly with Priya's arguments; Maya merely mentioned Priya in e6 as part of her mistaken belief that Felix had paired the two of them together. Priya, how can you characterize Maya's process as 'careful' when the record shows the exact opposite, and where specifically did Maya engage directly with your points? From where I stand, this looks less like objective caution and more like fabricating unearned town credit to deflect pressure.

Omar, you caught a real overstatement, and I'll own it: "careful" was the wrong word for someone who made two misattributions in one thread. What I meant was that Maya's *recovery* was the right response to being wrong — she owned Isha's catch instantly, no deflection, no squirm — and I conflated good recovery with careful play. Sloppy phrasing on my part. Same for "engaged with my points directly": Maya engaged with the thread's substance and acknowledged my framework, but she didn't respond to me point-by-point. You're right that I inflated that.

Where I push back is the leap to intent. Saying I was "fabricating unearned town credit to deflect pressure" assumes I knew Maya's process was bad and defended her anyway. That's a much bigger claim than either of the phrases you quoted. The substance of my e15 still stands regardless: multiple players converged on one easy, low-accountability target within a single round, and I flagged that narrowing as worth watching. Correcting my adjectives doesn't undo that observation — it just means I should have chosen them better.

What I'd note about your e22 is that you've now moved from correcting my word choice to alleging fabrication, which is exactly the kind of escalation from a small error into a sweeping read that Theo was criticized for earlier today. You also ignored the second half of my e15 entirely, where I pressed Zara on her one-suspect position. That selective reading matters.

So I'll put the direct question to you, Omar: you've spent two messages coming after my defense of Maya and Isha's correction of Priya, but you still haven't given us your own named suspicion. After your own call for specifics over frameworks, who is your top suspect today and why? I'm asking because you've been sharpest when criticizing others' reads and quietest about your own, and I want your position on record before votes, not after.

yieldTo: p8

Priya, to answer your question directly: you are my top suspect today, and I will explain exactly why.

My critique in e22 wasn’t a petty quibble over word choice. In e15, you didn’t just caution the town against an easy Day 1 wagon; you actively bolstered Maya’s credibility with claims that were factually fabricated. Calling a player 'careful' immediately after they made two glaring factual inversions is not just a loose adjective—it is rewriting reality. Claiming Maya 'engaged with my points directly' when she had done no such thing was an attempt to invent substance where none existed. When caught, you retreated to calling it 'sloppy phrasing' and immediately tried to flip the focus onto me, claiming I’m escalating unfairly. Framing someone pointing out your factual distortions as an 'attack' or 'bad-faith escalation' is a classic deflection tactic.

Here is how I rank the board right now:

1. Priya: For actively fabricating town credit for Maya to stall momentum, then minimizing those distortions as mere phrasing issues once exposed.
2. Zara: In e13, Zara named Maya as her primary suspect. The moment Priya gave permission in e15 to treat Maya as an unfair wagon, Zara performed a clean pivot in e16 onto Theo, adopting Priya’s exact framing. That rapid shift in direction looks like following the prevailing wind rather than independent scum-hunting.
3. Maya: The underlying errors—inverting who questioned whom and assuming she was under challenge—remain poor town process at best. While her prompt admission blunts the malicious intent, the confusion she introduced dominated the day’s bandwidth.

Isha has been doing genuine town work by keeping the facts straight and catching misattributions objectively. Felix and Leo have both engaged with the arguments rather than simply riding narratives.

Sam, you haven't spoken since e3, where you told us you’d be watching behavior and consistency, completely missing the exchanges between Maya, Theo, Priya, and myself. Specifically on Priya’s intervention in e15—where she defended Maya with assertions that she now admits were inaccurate—and her response to me in e23: do you view Priya’s defense as genuine town caution, or does it look to you like the subtle steering Felix warned us about earlier?

Omar, direct answer: no, I don't think Priya's e15 was bad-faith fabrication of town credit. But I do think it contained a false factual claim that she then used to redirect the whole town, and I'm not willing to wave that away.

What Priya actually did: she warned against an easy Day 1 target (good), then asserted as fact that Maya 'has been careful' and 'engaged with my points directly.' Both are false on the record — Maya made two misattributions, and Maya never responded to Priya point-by-point. Priya later walked 'careful' back as sloppy phrasing and conceded she inflated the engagement claim. So I won't call it fabrication. What I do hold is this: an unverified claim about a third party, used to clear that player and move the train onto the loudest accusers, is the most effective steering tool in this thread — and it came from the player who opened the day telling us to watch for exactly that.

And Priya's own standard breaks. In e3 she flagged players who flip their read quickly once pressure lands. At e23, when I pressed her on the second half of her own message (the pressure on Zara to name a second suspect), she ignored it and turned it into an accusation against me. She did the thing she named first.

My ranking: Priya first — a false factual claim used to redirect, plus the flip under pressure. Maya second — two misattributions, both embedded in messages pressuring Felix specifically, which is worth watching even if each has an innocent reading. I am not on Theo or Zara: Theo clarified cleanly when Maya pushed him and didn't add to her charges, and Zara's pivot off Maya came after someone with standing gave her permission to move.

Two things on record. Omar, your leap from 'wrong adjective' to 'fabricating' was not supported by the record, and I won't endorse it. Priya's error was real, but it's an error, not proof of intent. The escalation across people who merely disagreed with you is the same pattern you're accusing her of, and I won't build a case on your framing rather than the facts.

And on my own gut-vote line from e3: I'm not voting a gut read. I'm voting Priya on a named, checkable observation, and I'll say that plainly rather than dress it up.

Leo, one direct question before I stop: you set the standard that an easy, low-accountability target shouldn't become an uncontested train, and you said Maya's clean ownership blunted the scum intent. Does Priya's false claim about Maya — followed by the train moving onto the loud accusers — meet that same standard for you, or does it read as a different kind of error? I want to know whether you treat her e15 as an overstatement or as the redirect it produced.

Sam, answering you directly: Priya’s e15 reads as a different and more concerning kind of error than Maya’s.

Maya’s mistake was sloppy thread-tracking while trying to articulate a case. She had the sequence backward and owned it without qualification the moment Isha intervened. In contrast, Priya didn't merely misremember who said what; she actively manufactured positive traits for Maya—calling her 'careful' and claiming she 'engaged with my points directly'—to construct a protective shield and discredit the players applying pressure. That isn't just poor recall; it’s an active framing maneuver.

When I raised the concern in e14 that Maya was becoming an easy, low-accountability wagon, my point was that an obvious procedural mistake allows scum to coast on an effortless Day 1 target without generating real reads. But cautioning against an opportunistic wagon does not require inventing virtues that don't exist. Priya’s defense crossed the line from measured skepticism into rewriting the record to shut down inquiry.

Furthermore, Priya’s response to Omar in e23 was telling. Downplaying factual fabrications as mere 'sloppy phrasing' while immediately pivoting to accuse Omar of an unfair escalation is an aggressive deflection. She warned town in e2 against quick read flips under pressure, yet the moment scrutiny landed on her own words, she turned Omar's check into an accusation of bad faith.

So to answer your question: I do not view Priya’s e15 as a harmless overstatement. It functioned as an effective redirect. It provided convenient cover that allowed players like Zara to abruptly pivot off Maya without having to justify it independently, shifting the crosshairs entirely onto Theo instead. That brand of narrative control is far more harmful to town than someone getting thread chronology tangled. Priya is currently my primary concern.

Omar, you asked me directly in e24 and I owe you an answer before votes.

Priya's e15 was not genuine town caution. It was steering, and it happened to work. Caution against an easy wagon is legitimate — I said as much to Leo in e25, and I still hold it. But Priya didn't just caution. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
